issues.title: Abstract overstates the admissible matrix class

failure_location.quote: where $A$ is an invertible $M$-matrix and $b$ is a nonnegative vector. Existence and uniqueness of a nonnegative solution is proved.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: where $A=\alpha I_n-T_n(a)\in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with $a(z)=\sum_{i=1-n}^{n-1}a_iz^i$ and $\alpha =2-\|a\|_{\w} $ is an invertible $M$-matrix.
However, for a more general case where $A$ is an invertible M-matrix, more efforts are required.

issues.failure_explanation: The abstract claims existence, uniqueness, and computational results for an equation whose matrix A is any invertible M-matrix. The old body actually establishes its main finite-dimensional results after specializing A to the normalized Toeplitz form $A=\alpha I_n-T_n(a)$, and its own closing remark says that a general invertible M-matrix requires further work. Thus the advertised matrix scope materially exceeds the class supported by the paper.
issues.overall_effect: The abstract materially overstates the applicability of the paper, although the formal results in the body retain their inherited structural assumptions.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict every claim in the abstract to the structured class actually analyzed: A = (2 - ||a||_W)I_n - T_n(a), with T_n(a) nonnegative and the inherited norm hypotheses on a and b. Do not advertise the results for arbitrary invertible M-matrices.
issues.why_classification: The abstract advertises a central result for the full class of invertible M-matrices, whereas the proofs rely throughout on a much narrower normalized structured class and the paper expressly defers the general case. Aligning the abstract with the body abandons a substantial advertised model class, while retaining the advertised scope would require essentially new global analysis. Thus no complete route avoids either major scope loss or global reconstruction.

issues.title: Finite-support count does not determine the truncation cutoff

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we assume that the vector $v_A$ contains only $s$ nonzero entries.
$\widehat{v}_A \in \mathbb R^p$ is composed of the first $p$ elements of $v_A$

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that truncating $v_A$ to its first p coordinates preserves its 1-norm. The old assumptions establish only that $v_A$ has s nonzero entries and that $p\geq s$; they do not bound the indices of those entries. For example, a vector with one nonzero entry at an index greater than p satisfies the stated finite-support assumption but has a zero first-p truncation. The revision changes the assumption to prefix support, which supplies the missing index information.
issues.overall_effect: The displayed truncation identity and its repeated use are unjustified as written. The later upper norm bound can nevertheless be retained by using a truncation inequality, so no formal result needs to be discarded for this root alone.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use a support cutoff rather than support cardinality: choose s so that supp(v_A) is contained in {1,...,s}, and set p = max{s,t,N}. Then the first-p truncation contains all entries of v_A and the stated norm equality follows.
issues.why_classification: Finite support routinely supplies such a cutoff, so this local bookkeeping correction preserves the input class, truncation construction, norm bounds, and subsequent results. It is not a typo because the old argument genuinely uses the false implication that p at least the number of nonzeros must contain their indices.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: we assume that the vector $v_A$ contains only the first $s$ nonzero entries.

issues.title: Unexcluded zero right-hand side invalidates the endpoint proof and parameter bounds
issues.failure_explanation: The inherited conditions require only $b\geq0$ and strict upper norm bounds, so $b=0$ is admissible. At that input, $g(0)=\|A^{-1}b\|_1=0$, contrary to the proof's strict inequality, and the sign-change argument does not cover the endpoint as written. The theorem's conclusion is recoverable because $x=0$ is the unique admissible solution, but that case is not handled. Later bounds in lem:closed and lem:mu also contain $\beta/\|A^{-1}b\|_1$, which is undefined at the same admissible input.
issues.overall_effect: The existence-and-uniqueness proof omits one admissible endpoint, and the relaxed-iteration parameter contracts are undefined there. The entire nonzero-right-hand-side argument remains unaffected.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Handle b = 0 separately in the theorem, obtaining the unique admissible solution x = 0, and then retain the existing proof for b nonzero. In lem:closed and lem:mu, express the parameter restrictions without division, for example as τ||A^{-1}b||_1 ≤ β and τ(β - ||(A-βI)^{-1}b||_1) ≤ β, and verify the resulting trivial zero-input iteration.
issues.why_classification: This is an exceptional endpoint requiring only a short case split and denominator-safe formulation. The theorem's conclusion remains true, the zero-input iteration is elementary, and the entire nonzero-right-hand-side proof, method, and convergence guarantee remain unchanged.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: $b\in \mathbb R^{n}$ is a nontrivial nonnegative vector.

issues.title: Fixed-point iteration omits the scalar update
issues.failure_explanation: The procedure specifies $x_{k+1}$ in terms of $\mu_k$ and gives $x_0$, but it supplies no rule for $\mu_k$ or its initial value. Consequently, the display alone does not determine a sequence. The neighboring relaxed iteration and the statement that it reduces to fixed1 at $\tau=1$ uniquely force $\mu_k=\|x_k\|_1$, with $\mu_0=0$.
issues.overall_effect: The cited fixed-point procedure is not independently executable as printed, although the separately specified relaxed iteration and its analysis remain well-defined.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Augment fixed1 with the update μ_k = ||x_k||_1 for every k, so that μ_0 = 0 follows from x_0 = 0. This makes the recursion executable and makes it exactly the τ = 1 instance of the neighboring relaxed iteration.
issues.why_classification: The adjacent iteration uniquely supplies the missing scalar rule, and adding it is a short local repair preserving the intended algorithm. Nevertheless, the omission is not merely typographical because the printed recursion does not define a sequence until its missing state update is supplied.

issues.title: Taylor expansion understates the quadratic remainder

failure_location.quote: For any initial value $\mu_0\in [0,\beta]$, we have  $$\mu_*=h(\mu_0)+h'(\mu_0)(\mu_*-\mu_0)+o(|\mu_*-\mu_0|^2),$$

issues.failure_explanation: The prose asserts that after the constant and linear terms the remainder is $o(|\mu_* -\mu_0|^2)$. From the old formulas for f and h, differentiating once more gives a generally nonzero quadratic coefficient for nonzero b and positive $\tau$. The old material therefore supports an $O(|\mu_* -\mu_0|^2)$ remainder, not a remainder asymptotically smaller than quadratic. This is exactly the distinction corrected in version 2.
issues.overall_effect: The local convergence heuristic incorrectly suppresses the ordinary quadratic Taylor term. The parameter choice and all formal convergence results remain valid with a big-O remainder.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the two little-o remainders by O(|μ_* - μ_0|^2), and state that choosing τ to cancel the linear term leaves an ordinary quadratic local error. The parameter formula and the formal convergence results can remain unchanged.
issues.why_classification: The displayed formulas imply a generally nonzero second derivative, so the smaller-than-quadratic remainder is a coherent but false asymptotic claim. The correction is contained and leaves a recognizably comparable parameter-selection heuristic, but it weakens the claimed local asymptotic order from little-o of the square to big-O of the square. That limited rate loss exceeds a same-guarantee minor repair without requiring global reconstruction.

issues.title: Malformed parametrization of the perturbed matrix

failure_location.quote: In the rest of this section, we suppose $A+\Delta A$ is still an invertible $M$-matrix, in detail, we suppose $A+\Delta A=\widehat{a}I-T(\widehat{a})$, where $\widehat{\alpha}=2-\|\widehat{a}\|_{\infty}$ and $T(\widehat{a})\geq 0$.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: where $A=\alpha I_n-T_n(a)\in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with $a(z)=\sum_{i=1-n}^{n-1}a_iz^i$ and $\alpha =2-\|a\|_{\w} $ is an invertible $M$-matrix.

issues.failure_explanation: The setup claims to specify the structured perturbed coefficient, but $\widehat a$ is used simultaneously as the Toeplitz symbol in $T(\widehat a)$ and as the scalar coefficient of I, while the separately defined scalar $\widehat\alpha$ is unused. The earlier solvability setup instead requires a scalar $\alpha$ in $\alpha I-T_n(a)$, with its value tied to the Wiener norm. Thus the subsequent invocation of thm:solution is not licensed by the perturbation hypotheses as printed.
issues.overall_effect: The perturbation section lacks a coherent coefficient interface for its solvability assertion and ensuing bound. The underlying argument can be read consistently after correcting the parameter notation.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Write the perturbation parametrization as A + ΔA = widehat alpha I_n - T_n(widehat a), with widehat alpha = 2 - ||widehat a||_W and T_n(widehat a) nonnegative, followed by the already stated norm hypotheses.
issues.why_classification: The old source already uses widehat a as the Toeplitz symbol while separately defining the otherwise unused scalar widehat alpha, and the preceding solvability setup uniquely fixes the Wiener norm and matrix dimensions. The correction is therefore a source-forced repair of an ill-typed transcription, with no mathematical argument or guarantee changed.

issues.title: Numerical-performance comparison is reversed

failure_location.quote: In the first case, Table \ref{table2} shows that  Newton iteration is inferior to both the SDA and the relaxed fixed-point iteration in terms of the number of iterations and CPU time.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that Newton iteration is inferior to both alternatives in iteration count and CPU time. The old Table 2 actually reports Newton at 6 iterations and 0.5937 seconds, versus RFPI at 45 and 1.0535, and SDA at the same 6 iterations but a larger 0.8514 seconds. Thus Newton is faster than both, uses fewer iterations than RFPI, and ties SDA in iteration count—the opposite of the stated inferiority.
issues.overall_effect: The paper gives a materially false summary of its first numerical comparison, reversing the apparent performance of Newton iteration.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the sentence by the exact comparison in Table 2: Newton uses fewer iterations than RFPI, ties SDA in iteration count, and has lower CPU time than both methods.
issues.why_classification: The cited table directly and uniquely determines the comparison: 6 iterations and 0.5937 seconds for Newton, versus 45 and 1.0535 for RFPI and 6 and 0.8514 for SDA. The reversed prose is a transcriptional summary error requiring no repair to data, algorithms, or mathematical reasoning.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: In the first case, Table \ref{table2} shows that  Newton's iteration is {superior} to both the SDA and the relaxed fixed-point iteration in terms of the number of iterations and CPU time.
